error_description: A student inverted the part-whole relationship when attempting to construct an improper fraction, creating a proper fraction instead.
example: When asked to make a stick that is fourteen-eighths of an 8/8-stick, the student partitioned a stick into fourteen parts and selected eight, resulting in eight-fourteenths.

error_description: The student conflated the number of parts needed for an improper fraction with the whole unit, failing to coordinate the three levels of units necessary to form the improper fraction in relation to the unit bar.
example: When asked to make a 3/3-bar into a 9/8-bar, Bridget suggested making eight more 24-part bars 'so you'd have nine-eighths,' treating nine-eighths as a unit of nine units without forming eight of those units as equal to the unit bar.

error_description: The student struggles to name the length of a newly created fractional collection relative to the original referent unit.
example: After making a collection of 35 mini-parts, Michael calls the length 'thirty-five sevenths' and then 'thirty-five thirty fifths' before correctly deducing it is 11 and 2/3 unit bars.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students do not attach the proper reference unit to their fractional results, confusing a fraction of the total combined amount with a fraction of a single constituent unit.
example: After sharing four pizzas among three people, a student stated each person would receive 1 1/3 of the total amount of pizza, instead of recognizing that they receive 1 1/3 pizzas, which is 1/3 of the total original amount.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Prospective teachers possess a narrow understanding of division restricted to the partitive model, which hinders their ability to conceptualize division by a fraction.
example: Participants struggled to relate 1 3/4 ÷ 1/2 to a concrete situation because they only thought of division as forming a certain number of equal parts.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students judge the reasonableness of a fraction sum by mechanically checking if the resulting denominator is a multiple of the addends' denominators, rather than assessing the magnitude of the fractions.
example: When deciding if 5/8 + 4/7 = 8/15 is reasonable, a student rejected it because '15 is not a multiple of 8 and 7', completely ignoring that both fractions are around a half and the sum must be greater than one.
authors: Robert E. Reys, Barbara J. Reys, Nobuhiko Nohda, Junichi Ishida, Shigeo Yoshikawa and Katsuhiko Shimizu
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Because of a rigid reliance on always making a median cut first, children conclude that partitioning a shape into an odd number of equal parts is impossible.
example: When asked to make an odd number of parts like three or five, a child responds, 'I can't get it because it's not even' or 'It can't be done.'
grade_band_as_declared: kindergarten and the first three grades
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students incorrectly use the entire visible number line segment, rather than the intended segment from 0 to 1, as the reference unit.
example: When working with a number line labeled from 0 to 2, students' incorrect responses were consistent with incorrectly using the interval from 0 to 2 as the single unit.
authors: George W. Bright, Merlyn J. Behr, Thomas R. Post and Ipke Wachsmuth
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: The student interprets a fractional representation based on the part composed of fewer pieces, focusing on the nonshaded or missing pieces if they comprise the smaller part.
example: When shown an area model representing 5/6 (with 5 shaded pieces and 1 nonshaded piece), the student interpreted the fraction as 1/6 because 'There's like, all, except one shaded.'
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students fixate on using learned standard algorithms, such as finding exact common denominators, rather than employing flexible estimation strategies, often leading to frustration and errors.
example: Students attempted to mentally calculate common denominators for fractions, apologizing for the imprecision of their estimates and stating they could do better with a calculator or paper.
authors: Sheri A. Hanson and Thomas P. Hogan
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students who have not yet constructed a splitting operation may incorrectly iterate the given whole rather than producing a piece that could be iterated to reproduce the given whole.
example: When told an unpartitioned stick was 3 times as long as another stick and asked to draw the other stick, a student drew a new stick that was three iterations of the original stick.
authors: Anderson Norton, Jesse L. M. Wilkins, and Cong ze Xu
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students view the individual pieces resulting from partitioning as independent whole-number counting units rather than as fractional portions of a referent whole.
example: To find 1/4 of 1/2 of a cookie, a student splits the half into 4 parts, and reasons 'if this [one half] is four [pieces], this whole thing is eight [pieces], and I gave her one part out of eight,' treating the pieces as counting units.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students apply an incorrect algorithm to add fractions, typically by adding the numerators together and the denominators together.
example: Ted mentally computed the sum of 5/6 and 4/7 as 'nine thirteenths' by adding the top numbers and bottom numbers.
authors: Merlyn J. Behr, Ipke Wachsmuth and Thomas R. Post
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: A student attempts to solve equivalent fraction problems using superficial numerical patterns or inappropriate visual algorithms rather than operational partitioning schemes.
example: To solve 2/6 = /3, Alan guessed 4 for the numerator, arguing that '3 and 3 is 6, plus 2 more of 6 equals 12'.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students blur the unit when modeling fraction multiplication, confusing pieces of a single whole with pieces of multiple wholes.
example: A student explained 1/4 times 3 as 'like one fourth of a pie and then somebody brings two more... three pieces of pie that came out of four pieces of pie'.
authors: Keith R. Leatham, Blake E. Peterson, Shari L. Stockero and Laura R. Van Zoest
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students learn the parts of a fraction symbol as isolated counting procedures rather than understanding the fraction as a single quantity representing a proportional relationship.
example: A student stated, 'The top number is the numerator and that's the one that we chose stuff to put in, and the bottom number is the denominator and that shows all the things that are together.'
authors: Nancy Nesbitt Vacc and George W. Bright
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: A student struggles to understand why a fractional stick composed of multiple small parts is measured as an equivalent, simpler fraction by the software.
example: Josh creates a 4/18 stick and is surprised when the computer measures it as 2/9.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: When asked to iterate a non-unit fraction, a student may incorrectly multiply both the numerator and the denominator by the multiplier if they do not actively conceive of the non-unit fraction as an iteration of a unit fraction.
example: When asked to repeat a bar that is two fifths of a unit long four times, Kylie multiplied both the numerator and denominator by four, resulting in eight twentieths.
authors: Martin A. Simon, Nicora Placa, and Arnon Avitzur
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students inappropriately apply whole-number ordering strategies or rote computational procedures (such as cross multiplication) to compare fractions with the same numerator, failing to recognize the inverse relationship between the denominator and the size of the fractional parts.
example: When asked which is larger, 4/15 or 4/10, a student responded '4/15' and reasoned 'Because 10 is less than 15.' Another student reasoned, 'If you take 4 from 15 it's 11; if you take 4 from 10 that's 6. 6 is way smaller than 11.'
authors: Kathleen A. Cramer, Thomas R. Post, and Robert C. delMas
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students incorrectly justify the flawed 'add numerators and add denominators' rule by superficially combining their sketches.
example: A student claimed that 2/5 + 1/3 = 3/8 and justified it by drawing two separate sketches and combining the counts of shaded and total pieces.
authors: Donald M. Peck and Stanley M. Jencks
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students apply a whole-number ordering rule to denominators when comparing fractions, failing to incorporate the inverse relation between numerator and denominator.
example: One third is less than one fourth "because three is less than four."
authors: Merlyn J. Behr, Ipke Wachsmuth, Thomas R. Post and Richard Lesh
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students judge the size of a fraction by incorrectly comparing only the numerators, only the denominators, or the difference between the numerator and denominator.
example: A student may think 4/9 is bigger than 3/4 because 4 is bigger than 3, or that 3/5 is the same size as 5/7 because the difference between the top and the bottom in both fractions is 2.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students equate differing units when reasoning about rates, ignoring the specific fractional relationship given in the problem.
example: Ethan initially answered 4 miles for a problem asking how many miles one could hike with 4 cups if drinking 2/3 cup per mile, incorrectly equating 1 cup of water with 1 mile hiked.
authors: Victoria R. Jacobs, Susan B. Empson

error_description: Students interpret the visual representation of partitioned circles as whole, distinct shapes to be counted, applying natural number addition instead of viewing them as fractional parts of a whole.
example: When the teacher asks for the sum of a shaded third of a circle and a shaded quarter of a circle, a student says 'one plus one' equals 'two'.

error_description: Students intuitively generalize from their experiences with natural numbers that division is an operation that always results in a smaller number.
Students misapply concepts and procedures that are appropriate for whole numbers but inappropriate for fractions.
example: 6th-grade students typically claimed that 1/8 was greater than 1/6 because 8 is greater than 6.
authors: Martina A. Rau, Percival G. Matthews

error_description: A student expects the quotient to be smaller than the dividend when dividing by a fraction, due to overgeneralizing the partitive model of sharing to all forms of division.
example: When calculating 2 divided by 1/4, the student is surprised to get 8, arguing that dividing an apple 'in quarters' yields pieces smaller than the whole.

error_description: When encountering a new type of fraction multiplication problem, students initially felt they could not partition the composite unit because it was already partitioned.
example: Students responded that they did not know how to solve the new problem because 'It's [the composite unit] already cut up' or 'How can I get [X] pieces when I already have [Y] pieces.'

error_description: Preservice teachers incorrectly pose multiplication word problems for subtraction number sentences, confusing subtracting a specific quantity with taking a fractional portion of the remaining quantity.
example: For the subtraction sentence 4/5 - 1/2, a participant generated: 'Sandra has 4/5 of a watermelon in her fridge. Her mom comes to visit and eats half of the watermelon in the fridge', describing multiplication instead of subtraction.
authors: Helena P. Osana, Diana A. Royea

error_description: Students may assimilate fractions using a parts-out-of-wholes scheme based entirely on whole numbers rather than coordinating fractional units, relying on physically removing pieces rather than establishing a multiplicative size relationship.
example: When given an orange 10-rod representing 5/7 and asked to find 1/7, Dylan slid four red 2-rods away from a set of five and claimed the remaining one was 1/7, treating the problem as finding 5 minus 4 instead of recognizing the size of the unit.

error_description: Students believe that finding equivalent fractions by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number enlarges the fraction, resulting in a bigger physical quantity rather than an equivalent one.
example: TRAD students constructed rectangles of different sizes to show equivalent fractions, extending the rectangle further and assuming that more parts mean a bigger unit.

error_description: Students evaluate the magnitude of unit fractions by treating them as iterations of a unit of 1 rather than relative sizes to a fixed whole. This leads them to incorrectly judge that a fraction with a larger denominator is larger because it represents more iterations.
example: Isaac argued that 1/8 is bigger than 1/4 because 1/4 means 4 slices and 1/8 means 8 slices, later stating that 1/7 is bigger than 1/6.

error_description: When comparing two unit fractions, students incorrectly focused on the number of unshaded parts (the complement) left over in a partitioned unit rather than the size of the fractional part itself.
example: Student 3 argued that 1/3 is bigger than 1/2 because 'if you cut off one-third, it would have two more pieces left.' Student 5 similarly argued 1/3 is bigger 'because it has more blank sides than one-half.'

error_description: When fractional iterations exceed the whole, students whose fraction schemes are limited to partitive unit fraction schemes (or who lack iterative schemes) lose track of the original whole, resulting in renaming the improper fraction based on the number of iterations.
example: When a student iterated a 1/8 piece nine times to produce 9/8, the student referred to the result as "nine-ninths" rather than nine-eighths.

error_description: The student interpreted the numerator of an improper fraction merely as an instruction for how many pieces to divide the whole into, disconnected from the contextual meaning of fractional parts.
example: When told a bar was 5/3 of another bar, Barbara partitioned it into 5 parts, explaining: 'When you said it was 5/3, I thought that since 5 was the first number you told me, so that's how many pieces I would divide it into.'

error_description: Students believed that any two parts that combine to make a whole can be called halves, disregarding the definitional requirement that fractional parts must be equal in size.
example: Erik suggested that the purple and yellow rod could each be called one half of the blue rod, stating 'they're both halves, but only one's bigger than the other.'
authors: Dina Yankelewitz, Mary Mueller, Carolyn A. Maher

error_description: Children overgeneralize their whole number counting principles to fractions, believing that larger denominators correspond to larger fractions, or inappropriately adding numerators and denominators.
example: Believing that 1/4 is larger than 1/2 because four is larger than two, or adding 1/3 and 1/7 to obtain a result of 2/10.

error_description: Preservice teachers struggle to accurately partition a remaining fractional amount into a new set of parts if the number of remaining pieces is not already a multiple of the new denominator.
example: When Lizzie needed to partition two remaining parts into three equal parts to represent 'bills', she incorrectly represented three parts in the third row by drawing two of the three parts in the same size as the last third part.
authors: Jae M. Baek, Megan H. Wickstrom, Jennifer M. Tobias, Amanda L. Miller, Elif Safak, Nicole Wessman-Enzinger, J. Vince Kirwan

error_description: Students compare the magnitude of two fractions by treating their terms as independent natural numbers, concluding that a fraction is larger if its numerator and/or denominator are larger.
example: In comparing fractions with common numerators, students might incorrectly judge that 1/6 < 1/9 because 9 is greater than 6.
authors: Xenia Vamvakoussi, Wim Van Dooren, Lieven Verschaffel

error_description: When adding fractions, particularly mixed numbers, preservice teachers incorrectly add the numerators together and the denominators together, failing to find a common denominator despite mentioning it.
example: To calculate 1 2/3 + 3/4, Jillian wrote: "I would draw 1 and (2/3) plus 3/4 in a circle and take 1 plus 2 plus 3 over 3 plus 4, so my answer is 5/7."
authors: Cheng-Yao Lin, Jerry Becker, Yi-Yin Ko, Mi-Ran Byun

error_description: When dealing with fractional multiplicative comparisons where both the measure and the relationship are fractions, students may experience a 'quantity-measure conflict,' confounding the multiplicative relationship with the actual measure of the quantity.
example: When told a candy bar is 4/3 units long and is 8/5 the length of another bar, a student confused the two numbers, attempting to construct a bar that was 4/3 as large rather than working with the 8/5 relationship.

error_description: The student interpreted the union of two fractions by mentally segmenting the smaller fraction using the complement of the smaller fraction in the larger fraction, resulting in idiosyncratic unit comparisons.
example: Laura stated the sum of 1/3 and 1/4 was 'one and one third' because she used the 1/3 bar as her referent unit and saw the 1/4 bar as holding three smaller fractional pieces.

error_description: When comparing fractional parts of a whole, students may rely on figurative or perceptual judgments rather than operative reasoning, leading them to incorrectly conclude that visually different but mathematically equivalent fractions are not equal.
example: When asked how many eighth-strips equal three-fourths of a rectangle, some children approached the task spatially and figuratively, trying to physically fit the strips onto the 3/4 piece rather than using multiplicative logic.
mathematical_subtopic: conservation of the whole and parts

error_description: The student erroneously compares fractions by relying on whole-number magnitude rules, assuming that fractions with larger numerators and denominators are inherently larger.
example: Rachel chose 2/5 to be larger than 1/2 because 'for a start off the top number's larger, and the bottom is as well.'

error_description: Students erroneously add fractions by applying a flawed algorithm where they add the numerators together and the denominators together.
example: In solving a fraction addition calculation, Stefan uses the rule 'numerator plus numerator, denominator plus denominator'.

error_description: Pupils believe that equal fractional parts of a whole must be geometrically congruent, failing to recognize that non-congruent parts of equal area can also represent valid and equal fractions.
example: When asked to identify which shapes are divided into quarters, pupils typically only mark the shapes divided into four congruent pieces and reject shapes divided into four non-congruent parts of equal area.
grade_band_as_declared: fifth-grade pupils, between 10 and 11 years of age
authors: Tatjana Hodnik Cadez, Vida Manfreda Kolar

error_description: Students incorrectly claim that two fractions are equal in size if they both lack exactly one piece from the whole, focusing on the absolute number of missing pieces rather than the proportional size of the pieces.
example: A student claims that 'The fractions 5/6 and 7/8 are of equal size! There is always one piece of the whole missing.'

error_description: Students use natural number rules to order fractions, choosing the incorrect inequality sign because they reason based solely on the magnitude of the denominators.
example: When such pupils will have to complete an inequality like 1/8 ... 1/5 with the correct ordering sign (<), this dominance of meaning will manifest itself in the choice of the '>'-sign, because - as they reason - '8 is greater than 5'.

error_description: Children use a plus sign as a 'dummy number' or placeholder for 'half' in their written notations because they know a fraction must be represented by something, even if they don't know the conventional symbol.
example: When asked to make a notation for six and a half, Sheila wrote '6+', but explicitly stated that six and a half is less than six, showing the plus sign was not meant to denote addition.

error_description: Children inappropriately convert a continuous region model task into a discrete set model task after distributing pieces, identifying a share as one part out of the total separate elements distributed rather than a fraction of the original whole object.
example: After Claudia distributed four half-pizzas to four people, she incorrectly quantified each person's share as 1/4 because there were four separate pieces in total on the plates.
grade_band_as_declared: Year Three / third grade students (aged between 7.9 and 8.3 years)

error_description: Students assume that the base of a number system dictates the size of the unit whole, interpreting a base-fraction as a part-whole relationship relative to the base itself.
example: A student interprets 0.2 in base three as meaning 'two out of three' and compares it to 0.2 in base five, which is viewed as 'two out of five'.
authors: HELEN A. KHOURY AND RINA ZAZKIS

error_description: Students partially simplify fractions, leaving them in an incomplete form rather than reducing them to their lowest terms.
example: When asked to simplify 42/60, some students provided intermediate equivalent fractions like 21/30 or 14/20 instead of the fully simplified form.

error_description: Students encounter friction when their initial visual models and theorems-in-action, which account only for the first denominator, fail to accommodate the subdivision required for the second denominator.
example: When finding 1/5 of 1/3, a student who drew a 9x8 rectangle to easily divide it by 3 struggles to then divide it by 5, stating 'Splitting is the problem, now by 5.'

error_description: Students erroneously multiply instead of dividing when faced with division word problems or computations involving fractions.
example: To calculate 63 divided by 9/5, a pupil incorrectly multiplied 63 by 9 to get 567, then divided by 5, or multiplied 63 by 9/5 to get 113.40.

error_description: Pre-service teachers fail to distinguish between different subconstructs of fractions, incorrectly viewing problems where a fraction acts as a measure and where it acts as an operator as mathematically identical.
example: Concluding that the problems 'Petr got 3/4 of a cake. He ate 1/2 of the cake' and 'There were 3/4 kg biscuits in the box. Eva ate 1/2 of them' are identical problems, viewing the wording differences as a 'fruitless play with words.'

error_description: Students incorrectly compare the magnitude of fractions by calculating the difference between the denominator and the numerator, concluding that the fraction with the larger difference is the smaller fraction.
example: Comparing 2/7 and 3/7 by subtracting the numerator from the denominator (7-2=5, 7-3=4) and concluding 2/7 is smaller because 5 is greater than 4. Also applying this successfully to 4/9 and 5/7 (9-4=5, 7-5=2, so 5/7 is larger).

error_description: Students misinterpret the operation of dividing by a fraction, confounding 'dividing by half' with 'dividing into halves' (which actually means dividing by two).
example: The phrase 'dividing by half' is often interpreted as 'divided into halves', i.e., dividing by two.

error_description: The student initially struggles to assign a fractional quantification to a part if it cannot be used as a segmenting unit to exhaustively partition the given whole an integral number of times.
example: When asked what part piece b2 is of piece b1 (which represents one half), Ann states, 'this is not really anything, because you cannot fit one or two or three of this in one half.'

error_description: When looking for patterns in equations with equivalent fractions, students mistakenly compare the denominator of the first fraction to the numerator of the second fraction.
example: In the number sentence 1/2 = 4/8, a student notes that multiplying the denominator 4 by 2 gives the numerator 8.

error_description: Students assume that a larger number in the denominator represents a larger fractional amount, relying on their whole-number knowledge where bigger numbers denote larger sizes.
example: Believing a person who measured a window as 'six hand-spans' has a bigger hand than one who measured it as 'five hand-spans' because six is a bigger number than five.
authors: Jose Luis Cortina & Jana Visnovska & Claudia Zuniga

error_description: Students exhibit anxiety and make errors when working with fractions, struggling with the procedural steps of finding a common denominator and equating those new fractions back to the originals.
example: Students become confused when trying to relate fractions with a newly found common denominator back to the original fractions in the problem.

error_description: Preservice teachers believed that unequal pieces of a whole could not represent fractions at all, failing to recognize that unequal parts are still parts of a whole just not equivalent to each other.
example: The preservice teacher wrote, 'We also talked about wholes and how parts of fractions represent equal pieces of a whole, and if the pieces aren't equal, then the fractions would be incorrect.'

error_description: Students name a fractional part based solely on the whole number of unit items that make up the whole, rather than using the correct fractional name.
example: Naming the white rod 'ten' instead of 'one-tenth' because the orange rod is equivalent to ten white rods.

error_description: Students inappropriately conflate unit fractions with whole numbers when working with discrete sets, assuming the fraction's denominator represents the absolute quantity of items.
example: When asked to circle 1/3 of 12 marbles, a student circles exactly 3 marbles, considering 1/3 to be the same as the whole number 3.
authors: Xiaofen Zhang & M. A. (Ken) Clements & Nerida F. Ellerton

error_description: Prospective teachers generate incorrect equivalent fractions by applying mixed additive or incorrect multiplicative operations, such as doubling the denominator while halving the numerator.
example: When asked for a fraction equivalent to 18/20, a participant provided 9/40 by incorrectly doubling the denominator and halving the numerator.

error_description: Students misinterpret multiplication terminology in word problems, such as adding a fraction when the problem specifies a quantity 'times'.
example: Interpreting 'spent 2/7 of his money three times' as 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7.
grade_band_as_declared: senior class of elementary mathematics teaching
authors: Omer Sahin, Burcin Gokkurt & Yasin Soylu
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Teachers apply a flawed rule that a larger denominator automatically signifies a smaller fraction, regardless of the size of the numerator.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Failure to distinguish between the concepts of fraction and natural numbers when posing problems.
example: Ali has 1/2 pencils. His friend gave him 1/3 pencils. How many pencils does Ali have? [S28]
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Students incorrectly assume that dividing a number will always result in a quotient that is smaller than the dividend, failing to account for division by a proper fraction.
example: Predicting that (81405/67092) / (2884/3717) is less than (81405/67092) because they assume the operation of division must inherently yield a smaller number.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Students perceive the concept of fraction as limited, describing area models that are not divided into equal parts as valid fractions.
example: S4 describes an area model (a triangle) that is not divided into equal parts as a fraction 1/3.
authors: Fatma Gizem Karaoglan Yilmaz, Burçin Gökkurt Özdemir & Zehra Yasar
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Students utilize flawed, incomplete, or bizarre procedures to perform algorithms.
example: Calculating 125 x 1/5 as 1/125 x 5/1 = 1/25.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Students incorrectly interpret fractions using a part-to-part ratio rather than a part-whole ratio when analyzing partitioned continuous quantities or discrete objects.
example: When shown a rectangle with 1 shaded part and 4 unshaded parts and asked 'What fraction of this rectangle is shaded?', a student selects 1/4 (the part-to-part ratio) instead of 1/5.
authors: M. Di Gennaro, V. Picciarelli & M. T. Rienzi
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Prospective teachers reflexively convert improper fractions into mixed numbers instead of treating them as valid numbers in their own right, which limits their ability to use an iterative fraction scheme for accurate measurement.
example: When asked to draw a whole candy bar from a bar that is 7/3 as long, a PST changed 7/3 to 2 1/3 and visually split the bar to find 'roughly twice the size,' resulting in an inaccurate unit of measure instead of partitioning the bar into seven equal 1/3 pieces.
authors: LouAnn H. Lovin, Alexis L. Stevens, John Siegfried, Jesse L. M. Wilkins, Anderson Norton

error_description: When asked to find the whole given a proper fractional part, prospective teachers mistakenly find the fractional amount of the given piece instead of using the given piece to construct the whole.
example: Given a stick that is 3/7 of a candy bar, a PST partitions the given stick into seven pieces and disembeds three of those pieces, finding 3/7 of the given stick instead of letting the given stick be 3/7 of the whole.
authors: Alexis L. Stevens, Jesse L. M. Wilkins, LouAnn H. Lovin, John Siegfried, Anderson Norton, Richard Busi

error_description: Students face a discrepancy when dividing fractions using a visual measurement model versus the standard algorithm, confusing the remainder in terms of the original dividend units with the fractional part of the quotient in terms of the divisor unit.
example: Using a visual representation for 2 divided by 3/4, students find 2 groups with 2/4 of a whole left over (2 remainder 2/4), but applying the invert-and-multiply algorithm yields 2 2/3.
authors: Charalambos Y. Charalambous, Heather C. Hill, Deborah L. Ball

error_description: Learners exhibit the belief that all fractions must be less than 1, stating that a proper fraction structure is required for a valid comparison.
example: One PT commented that the fractions in problems #7 (5/6 vs. 6/5) and #10 (24/7 vs. 34/15) could not be compared because 'the [numerator] must be lower than the [denominator].'
authors: Eva Thanheiser, Dana Olanoff, Amy Hillen, Ziv Feldman, Jennifer M. Tobias, Rachael M. Welder

error_description: A student confounds the processes of fraction addition and fraction multiplication, seeking a common denominator first, multiplying the numerators, but inappropriately retaining the common denominator instead of multiplying the denominators as well.
example: For 1/2 x 2/3, the student converts to 3/6 x 4/6, multiplies the numerators to get 12, retains the denominator of 6 to write 12/6, and then reduces it to 2/1.

error_description: Elementary teachers incorrectly consider paper-folding activities as 'not mathematical' because they do not explicitly involve numbers, preferring instead procedural calculations of colored parts on grids.
example: In Czech schools this activity is unusual because many elementary teachers do not consider it to be 'mathematical' (i.e., not concerned with number) and prefer calculation of coloured parts of figures drawn on a grid...

error_description: Teachers struggle to accept that equal-sized fractional parts of a whole can be equivalent in area but different in shape (non-congruent), initially believing that differing side lengths preclude parts from being the same size.
example: The reason why I was getting stuck was that my mind said 'that the top of the rectangle was longer than the side of the rectangle, so how were they going to produce the same size?'
authors: P. Holt Wilson, Paola Sztajn, Cyndi Edgington, Jere Confrey

error_description: Prospective teachers hold misconceptions about multiplication of fractions, specifically struggling to write appropriate story problems that model the operation.
example: Writing inappropriate multiplication story problems for the expression 2/9 * 3/5.
authors: Tonya Gau Bartell • Corey Webel • Brian Bowen • Nancy Dyson

error_description: Students fail to perform operations correctly because they do not internalize or understand the mathematical meaning of the fraction symbol itself.
example: Students cannot perform 7 * 1/3 because they do not know what the fraction 1/3 symbolically represents.

error_description: Students inappropriately use a 'distance from the whole' (gap) strategy to compare fractions, concluding that the fraction requiring fewer additional pieces to make a whole is larger while failing to account for the size of those pieces.
example: When comparing 1/4 and 1/6, the student claims 1/4 is bigger 'Because it's closer to four than six', indicating that 1 is closer to 4 than 1 is to 6.
mathematical_subtopic: distance from the whole / gap strategy
authors: Meghan Shaughnessy, Timothy A. Boerst, Susanna Owens Farmer

error_description: When using fraction language to represent part-to-whole relationships in mixtures, students successfully identify the parts but erroneously equate the larger constituent with the whole.
example: There's one part pineapple and three parts water, so it's one third pineapple.
grade_band_as_declared: upper primary school age range (9–11 years)
authors: CHRISTINE HOWE, TEREZINHA NUNES and PETER BRYANT
journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

error_description: Students ignore that the size of the whole changes after an initial increase or decrease, failing to adjust the reference when calculating a subsequent fractional or percentage change.
example: When given a model that had been enlarged by a third, students incorrectly tried to restore its original size by reducing the new, larger model by a third (e.g., dividing 27 cm by 3 to remove 9 cm).
authors: JUHAINA AWAWDEH SHAHBARI and IRIT PELED
journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

error_description: Students incorrectly rely on rote written algorithms or cross-multiplication attempts to estimate the product of fractions, rather than using benchmarks.
example: Because 32 * 16 is larger than 21 * 7 by a lot.
authors: DER-CHING YANG, CHUN-JEN HSU and MING-CHIANG HUANG
journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

error_description: Students erroneously add the numerators and the denominators independently when estimating or calculating the sum of two fractions.
example: When asked to estimate the outcome of 12/13 + 7/8, students responded 19 or 21, or claimed that 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5.
grade_band_as_declared: fifth, sixth, and seventh grade (middle school)
journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

error_description: Students blindly memorize and apply procedural rules for comparing fractions or performing operations without conceptual understanding, often unable to explain why the rules work.
example: Since the numerators are the same, and one of the denominators is smaller, then that fraction is larger... I don't know. I memorized the rule I learned in mathematics class.

error_description: Students place a fraction on a number line by treating the entire length of the line as a single 'whole' to be partitioned, rather than locating the fraction's numerical value.
example: Marking 3/5 at the same place as the integer 3 on a number line that runs from 0 to 5.

error_description: Students interpret a fraction as a pair of independent integers rather than as a single mathematical object.

Teachers struggle to define the whole when multiple objects are shared, becoming confused about whether the resulting fraction should be named relative to a single object or the entire set of objects.
example: Teachers debated whether 2 pretzels shared among 6 children meant each child gets 2/6 or 2/12, at times incorrectly proposing that 2/6 and 2/12 might be equivalent fractions.

error_description: Students learn the standard algorithm for multiplying fractions as a rote whole-number procedure that is separated in their minds from their quantity-based operational models.
example: Nathan calculated 2/3 times 4/5 as 8/15 using the standard algorithm but could not connect this to his operational scheme, instead pulling out two separate fraction bars and stating he would put an 'x' between them.
